root.note: Italian guardare comes from a Germanic verb for ‘watch over’. Germanic w- often became gu- in Italian.

history: Italian guardare began as ‘to guard’ and ended up as ‘to look’. The ancestor is a Germanic verb meaning ‘to watch over’, brought by the Franks and Lombards. The Germanic w sound did not exist in Latin, and speakers replaced it with gu, so *wardōn became guardare, and the same thing happened in French garder. Over time the meaning moved from ‘keep watch’ to ‘look attentively’. Classical Latin had its own verbs, videre and aspicere, but Italian vedere kept only the sense ‘to see’, and guardare took the active meaning. So: guardo la televisione, I watch TV; vedo un amico, I see a friend. English ward, guard and warden are relatives, and so is Italian guardia.
historyEinfach: Guardare comes from an old Germanic verb meaning ‘to watch over’. First it meant ‘to guard’, then ‘to look at’. Use guardare when you look on purpose (a film, a picture) and vedere for just seeing. English guard and ward are relatives.

elsewhere.text: English got guard through Old French, and it also has the native word ward from the Germanic side. The two are doublets: the same root, with and without the Romance g.
